query: For an elemental Cr coating on a zirconium-alloy fuel-cladding substrate, what single intervention could prevent premature coating failure caused by elevated-temperature Cr–Zr interdiffusion while preserving protection under both normal subcritical-water operation and accident-relevant high-temperature steam? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism, predicts performance relative to the unmodified Cr-coated baseline, defines the relevant temperature, exposure-time, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a discriminating experiment and outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of Al to the elemental Cr coating (i.e. converting it to a Cr–Al alloy) will inhibit the high‐temperature interdiffusion of Cr and zirconium by promoting the in situ formation of a continuous, slow‐diffusing alumina (Al2O3) layer at the interface. This barrier will limit adverse interdiffusion during accident‐relevant high‐temperature steam exposure while maintaining excellent protection under normal subcritical-water conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Elemental Cr coating deposited on a zirconium-alloy fuel‐cladding substrate, which is prone to premature failure via Cr–Zr interdiffusion at elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor (~5 at.%) aluminum addition into the Cr coating to form a Cr–Al alloy.
generation.conditions: Normal operation in subcritical water (~300°C) and accident-relevant conditions in high-temperature steam (transient exposures up to ~850°C–900°C).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an adherent, continuous Al2O3 (alumina) layer along the coating interface.
generation.mechanism: Under high-temperature conditions, the Al in the Cr–Al alloy tends to preferentially oxidize to form a stable alumina scale. This oxide layer acts as a diffusion barrier that slows the interdiffusion of Cr and Zr, thereby reducing coating degradation while preserving the integrity and protective function of the cladding coating.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a pure Cr coating, the Cr–Al alloy coating will show lower levels of Cr–Zr interdiffusion, improved structural integrity, and sustained protection against oxidation and corrosion under both normal and elevated-temperature environments.
generation.baseline: An elemental Cr coating that suffers from premature failure due to significant Cr–Zr interdiffusion at high temperatures.
generation.boundary: Service conditions ranging from subcritical-water operation (~300°C) for extended periods to short-term high-temperature steam exposures up to approximately 850–900°C.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Al concentration and the precise high-temperature boundaries at which the alumina scale effectively prevents interdiffusion need further experimental refinement.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of zirconium-alloy cladding samples: one group coated with pure elemental Cr and another with a Cr–Al alloy coating (with ~5 at.% Al). Subject both groups to an accelerated oxidation test in high-temperature steam at 850°C for set durations, followed by extended exposure in simulated PWR primary water at ~300°C. After testing, perform detailed cross-sectional analysis of the coating–substrate interface using techniques such as energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to quantify Cr and Zr interdiffusion, assess the formation and continuity of the alumina scale, and evaluate coating integrity.
measurements: Elemental profiles across the coating–substrate interface (via EDS/TEM)
Adhesion and spallation assessments (e.g., via SEM)
Microstructural analysis of the protective oxide layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cr–Al alloy coating does not show a significantly reduced interdiffusion of Cr and Zr and does not display a continuous, protective Al2O3 layer (or its overall oxidation/corrosion performance is not superior to that of the pure Cr coating) under the defined test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: After the Fukushima nuclear accident, scientists have carried out extensive research on accident tolerant fuel (ATF) projects for pressurized water reactors (PWRs) []. Under the loss of coolant accident (LOCA), the cladding materials will be oxidized rapidly and cause immeasurable loss []. In comparison, ATF cladding can delay the time of fuel rod swelling explosion and reduce the rate of cladding temperature rise, which can greatly delay the progress of severe accidents []. For ATF cladding, the most critical demand is to reduce the high-temperature steam oxidation rate when an accident happens []. The main research direction of ATF cladding is divided into two strategies: the first one is to develop new cladding materials instead of zirconium alloys, such as FeCrAl alloy, SiCf/SiC non-metallic composites materials and Mo alloys [,,,,,]. The second one is to prepare protective coatings on the surface of zirconium alloy cladding to ameliorate its high-temperature oxidation resistance, mainly representing metallic coatings (Cr, Mo, CrAl, FeCrAl, high entropy alloy, etc.) [,,,], ceramic coatings (CrC, SiC, CrN, MAX phase materials, etc.) [,,,,,] and composite coatings (Cr/CrN, TiN/Ti

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have great potential as accident-tolerant fuel (ATF) cladding. Aluminum-forming duplex (BCC and FCC) stainless-steel (ADSS) is a candidate for ATF cladding, but the multiphase composition is detrimental to its corrosion resistance. In this paper, two single-phase HEAs were prepared by adjusting the content of each element in the ADSS alloy. The two HEAs were designed as Al0.05(CrFeNi)0.95(FCC) and Al0.25(FeCrNi)0.75(BCC). Their corrosion behavior under simulated pressurized water reactor (PWR) primary water was investigated. The corrosion products and corrosion mechanisms of these two HEAs were explored. The results show that the corrosion resistance of HEA alloys containing FCC is better than that of BCC and ADSS alloys. At the same time, the reason why the BCC structure composed of these four elements is not resistant to corrosion is revealed.
